episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Wild Spaces & Outdoor Life
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Wild Spaces & Outdoor Life.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who gets to call themselves local?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Temporary shutdown at Quesnel River Pulp will continue at least a little longer and Evening of Song to feature South Cariboo musicians on Music Creator Day, plus 14 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Who should own the risk of post-fire slope failure after containment is declared, and should that responsibility run on a funded, deadlined schedule like the fire line? Topics include: Post-fire slope failure after containment and who owns the risk, UK Burnham plan funding structure for crews versus landscape restoration, Climate trends in extreme rainfall and drought and their relevance to local planning, Weakening US forecasting capacity and the local warning and response gap, Cariboo Chilcotin rehabilitation projects, funding, and the scale of burned area.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Brain Injury Association

discussion.central_question: Who should own the risk of post-fire slope failure after containment is declared, and should that responsibility run on a funded, deadlined schedule like the fire line?
discussion.riley_position: The burned-slope hazard should be written into existing recovery plans with a named owner, and monitoring and maintenance should be folded into programs that already have staff and offices rather than waiting for new structures.
riley_key_evidence: UK Burnham plan allocates £45 million to fire crews and £25 million to landscape work including peatland restoration and farmland fireproofing
Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation's Palmer Project and Pressy Lake pilot have completed about 1,000 hectares of risk reduction work
My Cariboo Now reported over $5 million in wildfire risk reduction projects, including $902,900 for hand treatments in Puntzi, Redstone and Alexis Creek
discussion.casey_position: Post-fire slope risk needs a named owner with a deadline and a budget line that survives election cycles, because folding the hazard into general recovery programs means nobody actually owns it.
casey_key_evidence: Clinton's Resiliency Centre closed and recovery support is reduced to Monday drop-in hours at the Clinton Library through November
Lancet Countdown reports extreme rainfall affected 17.2 per cent of global land annually from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8 per cent in the prior decade
Clinton fire exceeded 66,000 hectares and Pear Lake fire reached 164,740 hectares, with Pear Lake only being held rather than contained
discussion.resolution: They did not reach agreement on structure: Riley favors writing the hazard into existing programs now and fixing structure next cycle, while Casey wants a dedicated named owner with a deadline. They agreed that monitoring needs a maintenance line, that cost figures for slope work are unknown, and that the real test is what gets funded.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: How large and how long-running was the Big Bar Complex fire that the Clinton recovery article covers, and what does the recovery support look like?
Findings: The Pear Lake and Fiftynine Creek fires merged into a larger Pear Lake fire in July 2026, reported by CBC at over 66,000 hectares (660 sq km) and forcing evacuation of hundreds of TNRD residents, with Kamloops providing evacuation support. The Pear Lake fire, which forced the evacuation of the entire town of Clinton, was later declared "being held" (CTV). By August 23, North Island Gazette reported it at 164,740 hectares and still out of control. Wikipedia lists the wider complex at about 186,738 hectares as of August 9, 2026. The figures come from different dates and possibly different boundaries, so treat them as a trajectory rather than a single number. The October 26, 2026 article (100 Mile Free Press, mirrored by Today in BC) says wildfire season is over but the TNRD Resiliency Centre, which operated out of the Clinton Curling Club, still offers recovery services for residents affected by the Pear Lake, Big Bar Creek and Fiftynine Creek fires.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue this is a success story of tech-enabled coordination: a fire that swallowed a town's evacuation routes was contained and followed by a structured, multi-agency recovery program. Casey should press on what "contained" means at 165,000+ hectares, and on the gap between the season ending and the grief, income loss and trauma that linger for a small community. Ask who is still at the curling club, and what happens when the funding runs out.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What does post-fire rehabilitation in the Cariboo-Chilcotin actually involve, and how is it funded?
Findings: BC Wildfire Service and the Ministry of Forests have announced rehabilitation work in the west Chilcotin, led by a Wildfire Rehabilitation Coordinator for the Cariboo Chilcotin Natural Resource District. Planned work includes burning roughly 400 piles of woody debris and unused log decks to meet rehabilitation objectives. A September 4, 2026 notice rescinded the area restriction for Poplar Creek. My Cariboo Now reported more than $5 million in wildfire risk reduction projects, including $902,900 to Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation for hand treatments in Puntzi, Redstone and Alexis Creek, $450,000 for treatment in Dragon Mountain Park near Quesnel, and $827,600 for the Three Rivers area. Forest Enhancement Society of BC (FESBC) funding and Natural Resources Canada support the work. The Palmer Project, a large rehabilitation effort in the Chilcotin led by Indigenous-led Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation, is among the largest of its kind in B.C. The Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation Pressy Lake pilot and Palmer Lake work have completed about 1,000 hectares of risk reduction. One source headline says the province funded 16 projects and another says 14, so verify the count before quoting it.
Suggested angle: Riley can make the case for the rehabilitation model, with Indigenous-led delivery, government and philanthropic co-funding, and mechanical and hand treatment that reduces future fire risk. Casey can question the scale: pile burning is smoke-producing and only partly addresses forest structure, and the budgets are small relative to burned area. Ask whether these projects restore wild spaces or just manage them for fire safety, and whether a planned rehabilitation timeline matches how long forests take to recover.

roundup.opening_frame: A news day of distant climate warnings and disaster policy, with a few close-to-home business and arts items up front.

stories.point: Millar Western's temporary curtailment at Quesnel River Pulp now runs to December 1, not November 1, citing weak demand, poor pricing and tariffs on Chinese exports.
Local musicians will perform two hours of live original songs at 100 Mile House's first Evening of Song at Martin Exeter Hall on Nov. 7.
The Quesnel and District Chamber of Commerce handed out its 2026 Business Excellence Awards at a sold-out evening on Oct. 17.
Several states have November ballot measures that would dedicate money to habitat protection or climate impacts, and one could reshape wildlife management in a mountain state.
A Nature meta-analysis of more than one million people identified 1,260 genetic variants linked to the Big Five personality traits.
Heavy rain triggered three landslides in Summerland's Garnet Valley this week, sending debris onto the Campbell family's field on slopes burned by the Bald Range fire.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both are wildfire stories about ground left vulnerable after the flames are out.

stories.point: The UK unveiled its first wildfire plan, offering RAF Chinooks and A400M planes to civilian fire services and up to £45 million for fire crew resources.
Investigators used DNA from a felled tree to trace bigleaf maple poaching in Olympic National Forest, after thieves accidentally started a wildfire in 2018.
Canada's Changing Climate Report 2026, published in September, projects the end of glaciers by 2100.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both turn to what climate change is doing to B.C. and Canadian landscapes and the disasters they bring.

stories.point: Despite wildfires, floods and heat domes, B.C. party campaigns have made few commitments to mitigating future disasters.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both are about heat reaching people, from B.C. heat domes to heat losses worldwide.

stories.point: The 2026 Lancet Countdown report estimates heat disrupted work worth $1.07 trillion in 2025 and urges governments to declare climate change a global health emergency.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both lead toward COP31, the climate summit in Turkey that Britain plans to attend.

stories.point: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended approval of the Jackdaw North Sea gas field and reaffirmed the UK's net-zero pledge for 2050.
The 2026-27 El Nino is forecast to rank among the strongest on record, raising drought risk in some regions and heavier rain in others.
AI tools are uncovering a flood of software bugs, and engineers are racing to fix them before hackers can exploit them.
A Nature study led by Brazil's National Institute for Space Research finds the Amazon often releases more carbon than it absorbs.
Hikers are campaigning to save two Appalachian Trail shelters that the National Park Service plans to tear down, saying they fall short of its safety standards.
EU agriculture ministers agreed a partial position on farm subsidy rules for 2028 to 2034 but left the budget unresolved.
Chiricahua in southeastern Arizona became the 64th U.S. national park in October, after being a national monument for more than a century.

roundup.handoff: Burned slopes can keep failing long after the flames are out, and someone has to own that risk. The deep dive picks up that thread.

deep_dive.central_question: When a burned slope keeps failing after the fire is declared contained, who owns that risk, and should it be assigned and timed the way firefighting is?
deep_dive.riley_holds: Post-fire slope danger is a known, plannable hazard that existing recovery programs can absorb once someone writes it into the plan.
deep_dive.casey_holds: Containment is being treated as the finish line, and until a named owner and timeline exist, the risk is left to families like the Campbells.

beats.claim: Slope danger after a wildfire does not end at containment, because burned vegetation leaves ground that erodes in heavy rain.
beats.evidence: Global News: three landslides in Summerland's Garnet Valley sent rocks, water and debris onto the Campbell family's property after heavy rain on Tuesday, on slopes burned by the Bald Range fire; the family said the danger did not end when the fire was contained.
beats.pushback: Riley: the Summerland slides are a known post-fire hazard that a standard step in recovery plans can handle, and the UK plan (Wildfire Today) already uses landscape money to fireproof farmland, so the tool exists and only needs to be applied.
beats.leads_to_next: If the danger outlasts containment, the next question is whether anyone has funded work on the ground at all, and the UK plan is the clearest announced example of a landscape line.

beats.claim: The UK has put a funded landscape line next to firefighting, which treats post-fire ground as a public responsibility.
beats.evidence: Wildfire Today: the UK unveiled its first wildfire plan at England's first wildfire summit, with up to £45 million for fire crew resources and £25 million for landscape transformation, specifically restoring dried-out peatlands and fireproofing farmland.
beats.pushback: Casey: the £25 million landscape line is smaller than the £45 million for crews, and the coverage describes a plan unveiled at a summit with no delivery dates, so it is an announcement rather than a record of work on the ground.
beats.leads_to_next: Money for landscapes only matters if the hazard is coming, so the next beat checks what the climate evidence says about rain falling on burned ground.

beats.claim: Climate evidence points to more extreme rainfall on top of drought, which raises the stakes for ground that burned this year.
beats.evidence: Stuff.co.nz and eco-business.com: the 2026-27 El Nino is forecast to rank among the strongest on record and raises the likelihood of drought in some regions and heavier rain in others, but does not determine local weather on its own. abc.com.py and rte.ie (Lancet Countdown): extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade.
beats.pushback: Riley: the same forecasts say El Nino does not determine local weather, so planning around a global average risks overbuilding for a single slope that may never see the rain.
beats.leads_to_next: Forecasts say rain is rising and matters for planning, so the question becomes whether B.C.'s political platforms commit to preparing for it.

beats.claim: B.C.'s election campaigns have made few commitments on disaster prevention, even after repeated fire and flood seasons.
beats.evidence: The Tyee: despite wildfires, floods and heat domes, campaigns have made few commitments on mitigating future disasters.
beats.pushback: Riley: a campaign silence is not a budget silence, and the Tyee piece is about platform promises, not what ministries are already funding, so the absence is not proof of inaction.
beats.leads_to_next: If platforms are silent, the test moves to the Cariboo, where rehabilitation work on burned ground is the real evidence of whether the province is planning after fire.

beats.claim: In the Cariboo Chilcotin, rehabilitation work on burned landscapes is about to resume, so local crews and land users will see the post-fire ground being worked.
beats.evidence: My Cariboo Now (Oct. 29): wildfire rehabilitation projects are about to resume in the Cariboo Chilcotin Natural Resource District, with offices in 100 Mile House, Quesnel and Williams Lake, meaning crews and land users will see work on burned landscapes close to home.
beats.pushback: Casey: resuming work does not show it covers slope stability, since the post does not say what the projects treat, so the restart is not evidence the slope risk has an owner.
beats.leads_to_next: Rehab restarting leaves open whether the people living beside burned ground keep support, and Clinton's recovery services show what happens to that support as the fire recedes.

beats.claim: Post-fire support for residents near Clinton is shrinking to a scheduled drop-in while recovery moves to a later phase.
beats.evidence: 100 Mile Free Press: the Resiliency Centre at the Clinton Curling Club has closed; a Resiliency Drop-in Centre at the Clinton Library is open Mondays 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. through November, with bottled water, donated quilts and referrals, and Red Cross case managers on set weekday hours for Big Bar Complex residents.
beats.pushback: Riley: moving from a centre to drop-ins and case managers is a planned transition to the next phase, and it keeps referral support in place rather than abandoning residents.
beats.leads_to_next: Recovery support is being scheduled down while the ground keeps moving, and that sets up the landing on who holds the post-fire hazard once the programs wind down.

set_aside: Canada Changing Climate Report 2026 glacier projection: too far out to bear on a post-fire slope question.
Lancet Countdown health-emergency framing and productivity losses: about global heat and health rather than burned ground.
UK Jackdaw gas approval and net-zero debate: energy policy, not post-fire ground.
Chiricahua national park designation: a protected-area status change, not a fire-recovery case.
Vox midterm ballot measures on habitat and wildlife management: conservation politics without a post-fire link.
Appalachian Trail shelter demolition campaign: trail infrastructure in the eastern U.S., not disaster recovery.
Amazon carbon-sink study: a tropical forest finding with no tie to B.C. ground.
deep_dive.cariboo_beat: Beat 5: the Cariboo Chilcotin Natural Resource District, whose rehabilitation crews serving 100 Mile House, Quesnel and Williams Lake are about to resume work on burned landscapes, so the question of who owns post-fire ground is tested right there.
deep_dive.landing: The conversation ends on a structural disagreement: should post-fire slope and rain hazard belong to a named agency with a deadline and a reporting duty, or be folded into general recovery programs where nobody is clearly responsible for the ground.
